Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 104, verses 1–9:

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The verse ﴿Woe to every scorer and mocker﴾ was revealed in Makkah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

(p-1654) Al-Waylu (woe) is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence. What justified beginning a sentence with it, although it is indefinite (nakirah), is that it is an invocation against them. Its predicate is ﴿for every scorer and mocker﴾. The meaning is: disgrace, or punishment, or destruction, or a valley in Hell, for every scorer and mocker.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Zajjaj said: al-Humazah al-Lumazah is the one who backbites people, and on this basis the two words have the same meaning. Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah said: al-Humazah is the one who backbites a man to his face, and al-Lumazah is the one who backbites him behind his back.

Qatadah said the opposite of this.

It is also narrated from Qatadah and Mujahid that al-Lumazah is the one who backbites people concerning their lineages.

It is also narrated from Mujahid that al-Humazah is the one who strikes people with his hand, and al-Lumazah is the one who strikes them with his tongue.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: he strikes them with his tongue and mocks them with his eye.

Ibn Kaysan said: al-Humazah is the one who harms his companions with foul speech, and al-Lumazah is the one who winks his eye at his companion and gestures with his hand, his head, and his eyebrow. The first meaning is preferable, and from it is the saying of Ziyad al-Aʿjam:

"You approach me with affection when I meet you, though it is false; and if I am absent, you are the scorer and the mocker."

And the saying of another:

"When I meet you out of resentment, while you smile at me, *** and if I am absent, you become the scorer and the mocker."

The original sense of al-Humazah is breaking. It is said: "he humaza his head," meaning he broke it. From this is the saying of al-ʿAjjaj:

"And whoever we crush his head, it is shattered."

It is also said that the original sense of hamz and lamz is striking and pushing. It is said: "he humazahu yahmizuhu hamzan, and lamazahu yalmizuhu lamzan," when he pushed him and struck him. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And whoever we strike his honor, he falls prostrate, *** upon his backside, face down or on his back."

Al-Barkaʿah is standing on four limbs. It is said: "barkaʿahu fa-tabarkaʿa," meaning he knocked him down so that he fell on his backside. So says al-Sihah.

The pattern fuʿalah indicates frequency, so it implies that he does this often, and that it has become a habit for him. Similar are duhakah (one who laughs much) and luʿanah (one who curses much).

The majority read humazatin lumazatin with a damma on the first letter of each and a fatha on the mim in both.

Al-Baqir and al-Aʿraj read with a sukun on the mim in both.

Abu Wa'il, al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Aʿmash read ﴿waylun lil-humazati al-lumazah﴾. The verse is general, encompassing everyone who is characterized by this, and its revelation concerning a specific cause does not negate this, for the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.

﴿Who gathered wealth and counted it﴾. The relative clause is either a substitute (badal) for "every," or in the accusative place by way of censure. This latter is more preferred, because a substitute requires that the substituted element be treated as dropped. Allah, glorified is He, described him with this attribute because it functions as the cause and reason for the scorning and mocking, which is his self-admiration with what he has gathered of wealth and his thinking that it is excellence, and for this reason he belittles others.

The majority read jamaʿa (with light pronunciation).

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with shaddah.

The majority read waʿaddadahu with shaddah. al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, and Abu al-ʿAliyah read it with light pronunciation. Shaddah in both words indicates multiplication, which is gathering one thing after another and counting it time after time.

al-Farra' said: the meaning of ʿaddadahu is that he counted it (ahsahu).

al-Zajjaj said: and ʿaddadahu means for the calamities of the times.

It is said: "aʿdadtu al-shay' and ʿadadtuhu," when you hold it back.

al-Suddi said: he counted its number.

al-Dahhak said: he prepared his wealth for the one who will inherit it.

It is also said: the meaning is that he boasted with its abundance and its number. The intended purpose is to censure him for gathering wealth, hoarding it, and not spending it in the way of good. It is also said: the meaning according to the light reading of ʿaddadahu is that he gathered his clan and relatives.

al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads it lightly, waʿaddadahu is conjoined to al-mal (wealth), meaning and he gathered its number.

The clause ﴿he thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾ is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah) explaining what precedes it. It may also be in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: he acts like one who thinks that his wealth will leave him alive and immortal, never dying.

ʿIkrimah said: he thinks that his wealth will increase his lifespan. The explicit mention in place of the pronoun is for rebuke and reproach.

It is also said that this is an allusion to righteous deeds, and that it is these that make their doer immortal in eternal life, not wealth.

﴿Nay!﴾ is a rebuke to him for that assumption, meaning: the matter is not as this man who gathered wealth and counted it supposes. The lam in ﴿he will surely be thrown into the Crushing﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, meaning: he will certainly be cast into the Fire and thrown into it.

The majority read la-yunbadhanna. ʿAli, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Mujahid, Humayd, and Ibn Muhaysin read la-yunbadhanna (dual form), meaning that he and his wealth will both be cast into the Fire.

al-Hasan also read la-yanbidhanna, meaning that he will cast his wealth into the Fire.

﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing is?﴾ This interrogative is for magnification and terrifying, as though it is not among the things that minds can grasp or understanding can reach.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained it, saying: ﴿It is the Fire of Allah, kindled﴾, meaning it is the Fire of Allah kindled by the command of Allah, glorified is He. Its attribution to the noble Name is a glorification and exaltation of it, and likewise its description as kindled. It was named "Hutamah" because it crushes and shatters everything thrown into it. From this is the saying:

"We struck Mus'ab with the staff on the day we broke his nose, so that he would be angered."

It is said: it is the sixth level of the levels of Hell; it is said: the second level of it; it is said: the fourth level.

﴿Which rises over the hearts﴾, meaning its heat reaches the hearts, overtakes them, and covers them. He specified the hearts although it covers all their bodies, because they are the seat of misguided beliefs, or because when pain reaches them, their owner dies. That is, they are in the state of one who dies, yet they do not die.

It is also said that the meaning of ﴿rises over the hearts﴾ is that it knows, according to the measure each one of them deserves of punishment, by signs that Allah has made known to it.

﴿Indeed it is closed over them﴾, meaning sealed shut, closed, as previously explained in Surah al-Balad. It is said: "asadtu al-bab" when you shut the door. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Ruqayyat:

"Indeed in the palace, if we entered, a gazelle, *** struck, its curtain closed over it."

﴿In extended columns﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ʿalayhim, meaning: they are situated in extended columns, bound therein. Or it is in the nominative place, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are in columns; or it is an attribute of muʾsadah, meaning: closed with extended columns.

Muqatil said: the doors were closed upon them, then fastened with iron stakes, so no door is opened for them, and no spirit enters upon them.

The meaning of the columns being extended is that they are lengthened, and they are firmer than short ones.

It is also said the columns are chains (aghlal) in Hell; it is also said they are shackles.

Qatadah said: the meaning is that they are in columns by which they are tormented. Ibn Jarir chose this view. The majority read fi ʿamadin with a fatha on the ʿayn and the mim.

It is said it is a collective noun for ʿamud (column).

It is also said it is its plural.

al-Farra' said: it is the plural of ʿamud, like adim and adam.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is the plural of ʿimad. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr read it with a damma on the ʿayn and the mim, the plural of ʿamud. al-Farra' said: both are sound plurals of ʿamud. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose the reading of the majority.

al-Jawhari said: al-ʿAmud is the pillar of the tent; its plural of paucity is aʿmidah, and its plural of abundance is ʿumud and ʿamad, and both have been read.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-ʿAmud is every elongated thing of wood or iron.

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Ibn Mardawayh have related through several chains from Ibn ʿAbbas that he was asked about the words of Allah: ﴿Woe to every scorer and mocker﴾, and he said: it is the one who goes about with slander, who separates friends, who incites between brothers.

Ibn Jarir related from him: ﴿Woe to every scorer﴾, he said: a slanderer and a mocker; he said: a backbiter.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him, regarding the verse ﴿Indeed it is closed over them﴾, that he said: "sealed shut"; ﴿in extended columns﴾, he said: "columns of fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Masʿud that he said: it is al-Adham (a black, dark thing).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: the doors are the extended ones.

Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, he said: He made them enter into columns, and they were extended over them at their necks, and the doors were fastened with them.

Ibn Jarir related from him: ﴿Woe to every scorer﴾, he said: a slanderer and a mocker; he said: a backbiter.

ʿAbd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn al-Mundhir also related from him, regarding the verse ﴿Indeed it is closed over them﴾, that he said: "sealed shut"; ﴿in extended columns﴾, he said: "columns of fire."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Masʿud that he said: it is al-Adham (a black, dark thing).

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: the doors are the extended ones.

Ibn Jarir related from him concerning the verse, he said: He made them enter into columns, and they were extended over them at their necks, and the doors were fastened with them.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 104, verses 1–9:

Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: The verse ﴿Woe to every scorer and mocker﴾ was revealed in Makkah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

(p-1654) Al-Waylu (woe) is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence. What justified beginning a sentence with it, although it is indefinite (nakirah), is that it is an invocation against them. Its predicate is ﴿for every scorer and mocker﴾. The meaning is: disgrace, or punishment, or destruction, or a valley in Hell, for every scorer and mocker.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Zajjaj said: al-Humazah al-Lumazah is the one who backbites people, and on this basis the two words have the same meaning. Abu al-ʿAliyah, al-Hasan, Mujahid, and ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah said: al-Humazah is the one who backbites a man to his face, and al-Lumazah is the one who backbites him behind his back.

Qatadah said the opposite of this.

It is also narrated from Qatadah and Mujahid that al-Lumazah is the one who backbites people concerning their lineages.

It is also narrated from Mujahid that al-Humazah is the one who strikes people with his hand, and al-Lumazah is the one who strikes them with his tongue.

Sufyan al-Thawri said: he strikes them with his tongue and mocks them with his eye.

Ibn Kaysan said: al-Humazah is the one who harms his companions with foul speech, and al-Lumazah is the one who winks his eye at his companion and gestures with his hand, his head, and his eyebrow. The first meaning is preferable, and from it is the saying of Ziyad al-Aʿjam:

"You approach me with affection when I meet you, though it is false; and if I am absent, you are the scorer and the mocker."

And the saying of another:

"When I meet you out of resentment, while you smile at me, *** and if I am absent, you become the scorer and the mocker."

The original sense of al-Humazah is breaking. It is said: "he humaza his head," meaning he broke it. From this is the saying of al-ʿAjjaj:

"And whoever we crush his head, it is shattered."

It is also said that the original sense of hamz and lamz is striking and pushing. It is said: "he humazahu yahmizuhu hamzan, and lamazahu yalmizuhu lamzan," when he pushed him and struck him. From this is the saying of the poet:

"And whoever we strike his honor, he falls prostrate, *** upon his backside, face down or on his back."

Al-Barkaʿah is standing on four limbs. It is said: "barkaʿahu fa-tabarkaʿa," meaning he knocked him down so that he fell on his backside. So says al-Sihah.

The pattern fuʿalah indicates frequency, so it implies that he does this often, and that it has become a habit for him. Similar are duhakah (one who laughs much) and luʿanah (one who curses much).

The majority read humazatin lumazatin with a damma on the first letter of each and a fatha on the mim in both.

Al-Baqir and al-Aʿraj read with a sukun on the mim in both.

Abu Wa'il, al-Nakhaʿi, and al-Aʿmash read ﴿waylun lil-humazati al-lumazah﴾. The verse is general, encompassing everyone who is characterized by this, and its revelation concerning a specific cause does not negate this, for the consideration is the generality of the wording, not the specificity of the cause.

﴿Who gathered wealth and counted it﴾. The relative clause is either a substitute (badal) for "every," or in the accusative place by way of censure. This latter is more preferred, because a substitute requires that the substituted element be treated as dropped. Allah, glorified is He, described him with this attribute because it functions as the cause and reason for the scorning and mocking, which is his self-admiration with what he has gathered of wealth and his thinking that it is excellence, and for this reason he belittles others.

The majority read jamaʿa (with light pronunciation).

Ibn ʿAmir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read it with shaddah.

The majority read waʿaddadahu with shaddah. al-Hasan, al-Kalbi, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, and Abu al-ʿAliyah read it with light pronunciation. Shaddah in both words indicates multiplication, which is gathering one thing after another and counting it time after time.

al-Farra' said: the meaning of ʿaddadahu is that he counted it (ahsahu).

al-Zajjaj said: and ʿaddadahu means for the calamities of the times.

It is said: "aʿdadtu al-shay' and ʿadadtuhu," when you hold it back.

al-Suddi said: he counted its number.

al-Dahhak said: he prepared his wealth for the one who will inherit it.

It is also said: the meaning is that he boasted with its abundance and its number. The intended purpose is to censure him for gathering wealth, hoarding it, and not spending it in the way of good. It is also said: the meaning according to the light reading of ʿaddadahu is that he gathered his clan and relatives.

al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads it lightly, waʿaddadahu is conjoined to al-mal (wealth), meaning and he gathered its number.

The clause ﴿he thinks his wealth will make him immortal﴾ is a new sentence (mustaʾnafah) explaining what precedes it. It may also be in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause (hal), meaning: he acts like one who thinks that his wealth will leave him alive and immortal, never dying.

ʿIkrimah said: he thinks that his wealth will increase his lifespan. The explicit mention in place of the pronoun is for rebuke and reproach.

It is also said that this is an allusion to righteous deeds, and that it is these that make their doer immortal in eternal life, not wealth.

﴿Nay!﴾ is a rebuke to him for that assumption, meaning: the matter is not as this man who gathered wealth and counted it supposes. The lam in ﴿he will surely be thrown into the Crushing﴾ is the answer to an implied oath, meaning: he will certainly be cast into the Fire and thrown into it.

The majority read la-yunbadhanna. ʿAli, al-Hasan, Muhammad ibn Kaʿb, Nasr ibn ʿAsim, Mujahid, Humayd, and Ibn Muhaysin read la-yunbadhanna (dual form), meaning that he and his wealth will both be cast into the Fire.

al-Hasan also read la-yanbidhanna, meaning that he will cast his wealth into the Fire.

﴿And what will make you know what the Crushing is?﴾ This interrogative is for magnification and terrifying, as though it is not among the things that minds can grasp or understanding can reach.

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained it, saying: ﴿It is the Fire of Allah, kindled﴾, meaning it is the Fire of Allah kindled by the command of Allah, glorified is He. Its attribution to the noble Name is a glorification and exaltation of it, and likewise its description as kindled. It was named "Hutamah" because it crushes and shatters everything thrown into it. From this is the saying:

"We struck Mus'ab with the staff on the day we broke his nose, so that he would be angered."

It is said: it is the sixth level of the levels of Hell; it is said: the second level of it; it is said: the fourth level.

﴿Which rises over the hearts﴾, meaning its heat reaches the hearts, overtakes them, and covers them. He specified the hearts although it covers all their bodies, because they are the seat of misguided beliefs, or because when pain reaches them, their owner dies. That is, they are in the state of one who dies, yet they do not die.

It is also said that the meaning of ﴿rises over the hearts﴾ is that it knows, according to the measure each one of them deserves of punishment, by signs that Allah has made known to it.

﴿Indeed it is closed over them﴾, meaning sealed shut, closed, as previously explained in Surah al-Balad. It is said: "asadtu al-bab" when you shut the door. From this is the saying of Qays ibn al-Ruqayyat:

"Indeed in the palace, if we entered, a gazelle, *** struck, its curtain closed over it."

﴿In extended columns﴾ is in the accusative place as a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in ʿalayhim, meaning: they are situated in extended columns, bound therein. Or it is in the nominative place, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they are in columns; or it is an attribute of muʾsadah, meaning: closed with extended columns.

Muqatil said: the doors were closed upon them, then fastened with iron stakes, so no door is opened for them, and no spirit enters upon them.

The meaning of the columns being extended is that they are lengthened, and they are firmer than short ones.

It is also said the columns are chains (aghlal) in Hell; it is also said they are shackles.

Qatadah said: the meaning is that they are in columns by which they are tormented. Ibn Jarir chose this view. The majority read fi ʿamadin with a fatha on the ʿayn and the mim.

It is said it is a collective noun for ʿamud (column).

It is also said it is its plural.

al-Farra' said: it is the plural of ʿamud, like adim and adam.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: it is the plural of ʿimad. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Abu Bakr read it with a damma on the ʿayn and the mim, the plural of ʿamud. al-Farra' said: both are sound plurals of ʿamud. Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim chose the reading of the majority.

al-Jawhari said: al-ʿAmud is the pillar of the tent; its plural of paucity is aʿmidah, and its plural of abundance is ʿumud and ʿamad, and both have been read.

Abu ʿUbaydah said: al-ʿAmud is every elongated thing of wood or iron.
